title: 6.4 Conductors in Electrostatic Equilibrium
text:
No. Doing so would mean a violation of Gauss’s law. Plimpton and Lawton did not detect any flow and, knowing the sensitivity of their electrometer, concluded that if the radial dependence in Coulomb’s law were 1/r(2+δ)1/r(2+δ), δδ would be less than 2×10−92×10−9^1. More recent measurements place δδ at less than 3×10−163×10−16^2, a number so small that the validity of Coulomb’s law seems indisputable.
If the electric field had a component parallel to the surface of a conductor, free charges on the surface would move, a situation contrary to the assumption of electrostatic equilibrium. Therefore, the electric field is always perpendicular to the surface of a conductor.
